issues.title: Bound shutdown after termination signal
issues.body:
This change prevents Xray from waiting indefinitely during graceful shutdown after receiving SIGTERM or interrupt.

Previously, shutdown depended on the deferred server.Close() call returning. If any feature Close() path blocked, the process could stay alive while listeners or active connections continued operating. This made stale Xray processes difficult to detect, especially when another process could bind the same port.

Now Xray runs server.Close() explicitly after receiving a termination signal and waits up to 10 seconds. If shutdown does not complete in time, the process exits with code 1 so supervisors can treat it as a failed shutdown and avoid leaving a functional stale process behind.

This issue was most visible on mobile clients. Some apps, such as Telegram proxy-style traffic, may continue using an already-established path even when the VPN/client UI appears disabled. If the old Xray process remains alive during a stuck shutdown, those connections can continue transferring traffic and updating usage counters, making the node look stopped from the client side while traffic is still flowing server-side.

issues.title: TLS : tls spoofing
issues.body:
fix #5964

### RawPacket aka TLS Spoofing

So first lets talk about the idea,

when you connect to a xray server, the censors can see your TLS ClientHello, read the SNI, and figure out what you are doing and block :)

The RawPacket aka TLS spoofing fixes that by injecting a fake TLS ClientHello before the real one Hits.


The fake one carries like a decoy domain (ex. baidu.com) and then the real one carries your actual destination (ex. www.example.com).

A sensor that captures the first packet sees baidu.com and think that you are just browsing, and everything is okay with that, but in reality your connection goes through :)


It can be configured in the `finalmask.tcp` okay? and its only for client side.


### How everything works


When Xray dials a TCP connection and the first `Write()` happens (which also triggers the real TLS handshake) , our Raw Packet setup does the following.

1.builds a fake Tls ClientHello with whatever SNI you want or you have option to provide the raw bytes (b64).

2.Then we. wrap it in a raw TCP/ip packet.

3.Then deliberately we corrupt the TCP header using whatever method is selected okay?

4. Then we shoot it out via a raw socket

5. Then immediately let the real `Write()` go through normally


In short : two packets arrive at the server back to back and the fake one gets dropped by the servers TCP stack because of the corruption and then the real handshake proceeds like nothing happened.


### Config Example

```json
{
  "streamSettings": {
    "finalmask": {
      "tcp": [
        {
          "type": "rawpacket",
          "settings": {
            "sni": "baidu.com",
            "payload": "",
            "method": "wrong-sequence",
            "ttl": 3,
            "count": 1
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```


### Available Fields

`sni` : The domain to put in the fake ClientHello. If you set this, it will auto generate a valid TLS ClientHello for you automatically. If you set `payload` and `sni` same time , sni wins here.

```
"sni": "baidu.com"
```

`payload` : If you don't want an auto gnrated ClientHello, then just encode your raw bytes that you want into base64 and put them here. I have added an option to do it from command line also. Do like this 

```
 xray tls fake-hello google.com
 ```

It will out the thing and then just copy paste.


Note : If `sni` and payload are empty or not set , the raw packet does nothing and the connection goes through normally.


`method` : It defines how we corrupt the fake packet so the server drops it.

`wrong-sequence` : It duplicates the sequence number (looks like a retransmission so server drops it)

So we grab the kernels `snd_nxt` ( the next sequence number the kernel expects to send), then subtract the length of the fake payload and then use that as the sequence number of the injected packet. The results then is a duplicate of the. last segment, so the receivers TCP stack sees it as a retransmit at best, or like out of window at worst and then drops it.


`wrong-checksum`: It flips all the bits in the TCP checksum (so server sees a bad checksum and drops it)

We build the packet with a correct checksum and then flip every bit(^0xFFFF). The receiver then validates the checksum and its wrong, so the packet goes in trash.

`wrong-ack`: It sets ACK number way outside the receive window (so server sends dup ACK then drops it)

It sets the ACK number to `rcv_nxt - window/2` and that's way outside of the receivers window, and the kernel responds with a dup ACK containing the correct sequence number, then drops it.

`wrong-md5` : This adds a fake TCP MD5 signature option and server without MD5 drops it

issues.body:
Fixes #7428.

XDRIVE's S3 cleanup deletes the session key before listing its children. On a backend that rejects deletion of nonempty directories, the first DELETE returns HTTP 412 and cleanup stops. This change collects the keys under the session prefix across all list pages and deletes them in reverse lexicographic order. Each child is deleted before its directory marker, and the session key is deleted last. Cleanup holds one key string per listed object in memory.

## Reproduction

`TestS3DeleteNonemptyDirectory` uses the production S3 client against a local HTTP test server. The server returns 412 for a DELETE while the directory has children. It lists the `abc/up/` marker on the first page and its segment on the second. After deleting session `abc`, the test checks that the only remaining key belongs to the neighboring session `abcd`.

To reproduce on the base commit, run these commands from the PR checkout. They copy the new test into a temporary copy of the original source tree.

```sh
before=$(mktemp -d)
git archive 82b5b76b | tar -x -C "$before"
cp transport/internet/xdrive/s3_test.go "$before/transport/internet/xdrive/"
(cd "$before" && go test -count=1 -run '^TestS3DeleteNonemptyDirectory$' ./transport/internet/xdrive)
```

On `82b5b76b` this fails with `S3 DELETE answered 412` on the first DELETE.

## Verification

On `5bebf4e6` the regression test passed 50 consecutive runs under the race detector. The XDRIVE package tests, CLI build and repository format check also passed.

```sh

go build -o /dev/null ./main
go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./
```

issues.title: XDRIVE: Cancel pending storage operations on interrupt
issues.body:
## Problem

`common.Interrupt` falls back to `Close()` for an XDRIVE connection. `Close()` drains the writer before canceling the connection context. If storage is holding an upload, interruption waits for the very operation it needs to cancel. The asynchronous slot announcement also uses a background context, so it can remain pending after connection shutdown.

svlavr reported both behaviors while testing direct VLESS multiplexing. A mock backend reproduced them with a held upload and a held announcement. [Original report in #7415](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7415#issuecomment-6886431076)

## Design

`Interrupt()` cancels the session before entering the existing `Close()` path. Cancellation runs before the `sync.Once` guard, so it can wake a graceful close that is already waiting. Both slot and WAL writers stop admitting work after cancellation and wait for in-flight writes to finish unwinding before storage is released. A canceled drain skips the EOF marker.

The slot announcement now uses the session context and is part of the writer’s existing wait group. The context makes an interrupted publication cancelable. Joining it also lets a short graceful transfer finish publishing its session before `Close()` sends EOF and releases storage. This keeps the inline first-segment optimization and the existing wire format.

`Close()` still means graceful drain. Transport owners use `common.Interrupt` on the underlying connection when they need to abort. The direct Mux proposal already unwraps stats connections on its explicit interrupt path. [#7364](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7364)

## Validation

- Added regressions for interrupting an already-running `Close()` with a blocked slot or WAL upload, canceling a pending announcement, and allowing the announcement to finish during graceful close. All four cases detect the original behavior on upstream `main`.
- Passed the full XDRIVE suite on Windows with and without `-race`, plus 50 race-enabled repetitions of the shutdown regressions.
- Trial-merged this branch with #7415 and ran both sets of regressions together 10 times under `-race`. Live cloud tests were skipped.

issues.body:
Follow-up to #7402, rebased onto `main` after both #7402 and #7430 merged: this is no longer a stacked draft, the diff is four commits, and it also settles the delay question and the compression side effect that #7402 left behind.

1. **Bound padding schedules and cancel their pauses on Close** (unchanged from the draft). Padding pauses are timers that watch a per-connection `done` channel; a configured schedule is rejected above 256 turns, 64 MiB of turns, or the handshake deadline minus ten seconds of pauses; an explicit empty `paddings` array (or `"noPadding": true`) disables padding, and an absent field keeps the preset.

2. **Pause before a padding turn and never after the last one**. A configured `delay` used to be applied *after* its turn, so the last turn of a schedule paused even though nothing followed it: with `delay: "300"` on the final turn the first proxied packet went out 300 ms later, while both ends otherwise waited for nothing. The pause now leads into the turn it is configured on - a captured gap is written on the turn that follows it - and the last turn is not followed by a pause. Which value each end waits is unchanged and now stated in the proto comment: the side that sends the turn samples `[delay_min, delay_max]`, the peer spends exactly `delay_min` (it waits the minimum, not "at least" it), so a range jitters only the sending side and `delay_min == delay_max` reproduces a captured gap.

3. **State what a configured padding list replaces**. Two decisions only lived in the pull request: a configured list is the complete schedule, so the preset's Play-state join tail runs only with the preset; and a peer cannot be checked for arriving early, because the turns are ordinary Minecraft packets that carry nothing to compare an early arrival against, with the pause bound covering a stalled peer. Both are now next to the code and pinned by a test.

4. **Never compress the frames XMC writes**. After `Set Compression` the writer deflated everything at or above the threshold, which is exactly the padding (zeros, ~300:1) and the proxied bytes (already compressed or encrypted): the padded shape disappeared and the CPU work bought nothing. The writer now always sends the uncompressed variant, which vanilla accepts at any size (`Data Length = 0` is not subject to the threshold check), and the reader still inflates what a real server sends.

That is why point 3 no longer says the peer's turns stay in the stream for the next reader: they are read and dropped by that reader, while the pause limit still bounds a stalled peer. This branch is rebased onto #7430, and the two changes coexist - the reader drains, and the schedule still spends `delay_min` on the peer's turn. issues.title: Happy Eyeballs: add successDefinition to race until TLS handshake completes
issues.body:
## Motivation

When the server's domain resolves to several IPs, Happy Eyeballs is supposed to pick a working one. In Russia, however, some ISPs (the DPI boxes installed at them) drop the ServerHello for some of these IPs while TCP to them still connects. Which IPs are affected differs from one ISP and region to another and changes over time: an IP that is blocked for one client works for another, so removing it from DNS would only break it for everyone else. Happy Eyeballs today ends the race at the first TCP connection, so it happily picks such an IP, and then the TLS or REALITY handshake can never complete. A retry usually picks the same IP again, because it wins the TCP race again. In this situation the current Happy Eyeballs is of no use at all, even though other IPs of the same domain work fine.

## What this PR adds

A new optional field `successDefinition` in `sockopt.happyEyeballs`:

| Value | The race is won by |
|---|---|
| `tcpConnected` (default) | the first established TCP connection, as before |
| `tlsHandshakeComplete` | the first connection that completes the TLS or REALITY handshake |

```json
"sockopt": {
  "domainStrategy": "UseIP",
  "happyEyeballs": {
    "tryDelayMs": 250,
    "maxConcurrentTry": 4,
    "successDefinition": "tlsHandshakeComplete"
  }
}
```

Without `successDefinition`, or with `tcpConnected`, nothing changes. Without TLS or REALITY, `tlsHandshakeComplete` is the same as `tcpConnected`.

The behaviour follows section 6.1 of Happy Eyeballs v3, which says clients SHOULD wait for the TLS handshake to complete before canceling other attempts: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-happy-happyeyeballs-v3/
Chromium's Happy Eyeballs v3 implementation does the same: a TCP-based attempt runs the TLS handshake inside it and completes only when the handshake does, and an attempt counts as slow (so the next one starts) if TCP and TLS together take longer than the connection attempt delay:
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/socket/tls_stream_attempt.cc
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/http/http_stream_pool_attempt.cc

Happy Eyeballs v3 is still a draft, and browsers do not use it by default yet: in Chromium it is behind the `HappyEyeballsV3` feature, which is disabled by default, and Firefox enables it only in Nightly.

## How it works

- The scheduler of `TcpRaceDial` is reused as is (`tryDelayMs`, `maxConcurrentTry`, `prioritizeIPv6`, `interleave`); only the attempt it runs differs. With `tcpConnected` the attempt is the same system dial as before.
- With `tlsHandshakeComplete` every attempt goes through TCP dial to one IP → FinalMask (if any) → the transport's own TLS or REALITY handshake. Only the TCP destination changes from attempt to attempt; masks apply to each attempt separately, exactly as on a normal dial.
- An attempt keeps its `maxConcurrentTry` slot until its handshake ends, and a hanging handshake does not stop the scheduler from starting the next attempt after `tryDelayMs`.
- Losing attempts are stopped by closing their connections. Transports that leave the handshake to the first write (gRPC, and HTTPUpgrade and XHTTP with Go TLS) get it completed inside the race, so a connection is never handshaked twice.
- The race happens under the same conditions as the TCP race in `DialSystem`: `domainStrategy` set, at least two IPs, no `dialerProxy`, non-zero `tryDelayMs` and `maxConcurrentTry`. Otherwise the transport dials exactly as before.

All covered transports now dial through `internet.DialTCPWithHandshake(ctx, dest, streamSettings, handshake)`. `handshake` is a function that wraps the TCP connection with the transport's TLS or REALITY client; it holds the same code the transport used to run right after its own TCP dial.

Transports covered: RAW (TLS, REALITY), WebSocket, HTTPUpgrade, gRPC (TLS, REALITY), XHTTP over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 (TLS, REALITY), MASQUE over HTTP/2. For XHTTP the race runs once per new physical connection. UDP

issues.title: Routing: add server-only VMess UUID routes and online user cache
issues.body:
Allow ordinary VMess clients to select declared server-side routes by changing UUID bytes 7 and 8, with only the server upgraded and no account flag required. `userRoute` is the shared routing matcher; `vlessRoute` keeps its existing behavior.

README.md is unchanged in the PR diff.

## Behavior and compatibility

- Generate aliases only for explicit `routing.rules[].userRoute` values applicable to the inbound and user, including existing exact/regexp user matching. Destination-dependent conditions remain routing conditions; Lua-only routing declares no aliases.
- Preserve exact configured UUIDs and the original account's email, policy, statistics and API identity. The experimental account flag and wire extension have been removed completely. Account JSON/protobuf definitions and client encoding match the pre-feature source; no account option or wire field is added.
- Admit connections after normal authenticated header checks. Registration IDs, route generations and pending-change checks reject stale candidates across account/rule changes, including removal and re-addition of the same account object. Closed validators cannot rebuild catalogs.
- Retain identity history during an inbound's lifetime so a removed exact credential cannot become another user's generated alias. Different original route bytes mark the 14-byte identity ambiguous and disable its aliases. Exact credentials remain usable. History is not persisted: independently revocable users and credential rotations must use distinct non-route UUID bytes.
- Align Unicode email removal with the inbound's lowercase index. Retain AuthID replay entries for the full inclusive timestamp-validity interval using 241-second buckets; accepted clock skew and wire encoding remain unchanged. This retains more replay records under sustained traffic.

## Cache and resource bounds

Only authenticated online/recent accounts populate the prepared cache; there are no IP/source-address hints. Idempotent connection leases expire two minutes after the final close. Route changes preserve live leases and idle deadlines without refreshing recency. Search and eviction share one recency list, immutable provider declarations are copied before filtering, and rejected cache growth does not evict unrelated entries.

Per inbound: 64 MiB prepared-key payload, a 128 MiB raw-alias-key limit, and two concurrent alias scans. Oversized live catalogs preserve exact credentials while rejecting aliases. Metadata, replay records and temporary old/new catalog overlap are additional memory. Occupied scan slots can reject further alias handshakes, including hot-cache users; exact credentials bypass those slots.

The amd64 AES-NI/SSE4.1 search accelerator retains all ten AES rounds in a 68-byte schedule and rechecks candidates with the standard-library decoder. Unsupported CPUs, `purego`, and Go FIPS mode select the standard-library fallback. This is not a cryptographic certification or a claim of VLESS-equivalent lookup cost.

## Validation

- VMess, router/command, routing features and configuration tests passed, along with the complete VMess `purego` tests and repository formatting.
- After removing the experimental account flag, all 160 published-binary compatibility cases passed again using clients 1.8.24, 25.12.8 and 26.11.9: 120 ordinary VMess/VLESS cases in both directions, 33 UUID-only/negative/legacy-route cases, and seven byte-identical old-config compilation cases. Coverage includes TCP/UDP, AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305, Mux, and route values 0/300/65535.
- Known-answer AES plus 4,096 differential decryptions; malformed headers and replay; identity collisions/revocation; concurrent account/rule changes; and 4,000-operation cache lifecycle checks passed. Selected regressions also passed 30 repetitions at each of 1/2/4 CPUs with shuffled order, Go pointer checking, and runtime CPU-feature fallback.
- Windows executable and Linux amd64/arm64 VMess cross-builds passed. The full network scenario package passed

issues.title: transport/internet/udp/dispatcher.go: Avoid info-level read failure after local session termination; Fix race
issues.body:
When the UDP idle timer or owner closes a session while `handleInput` is reading, termination cancels the context and interrupts the pipe. The read can return `io.ErrClosedPipe` after the loop's context check, producing an info-level `failed to handle UDP input` message for a local close.

Downgrade that error to debug only when this connection's local termination flag is set. Make the existing flag atomic because termination, input handling, and dispatcher reuse inspect it across goroutines. Unrelated read errors, closed-pipe errors without local termination, and parent cancellation alone retain the existing logging behavior. EOF handling and cleanup order are unchanged.

Tests exercise the real pipe interruption path, idle timeout, concurrent/repeated close, wrapped errors, unrelated errors during shutdown, parent cancellation, EOF, and the close callback count. The regression test fails on unmodified main with the original info-level message.

Validation on Windows/amd64:
- `go test ./transport/internet/udp -count=1` passed.
- `go test ./transport/internet/udp -run TestHandleInputTermination -count=100` passed.
- `go vet ./transport/internet/udp` and `git diff --check` passed.
- Local race-detector execution was unavailable: the environment has no CGO C compiler. Linux runtime tests were not run locally.

Refs #4621. This addresses local UDP termination only; it does not suppress remote resets or change general connection-error handling.

issues.title: XMC finalmask: Switch to native frame padding (breaking); `delay` supports range (receiver waits at least minimal ms)
issues.body:
Follow-up to #6769 (merged in `5d17b872`): completes the remaining `delay` requirement and, per [this reply](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7402#issuecomment-6890345279), switches padding to the more realistic wire format even though that is a breaking change.

## Delay

- `delay` is now a **string**: `"100"` or `"50-150"` (milliseconds). A number written against #6769 no longer parses, so this is a configuration-level breaking change as well.
- The sender waits a uniformly sampled value in `[min, max]` after its turn.
- The receiver waits at least `min` after each turn, including the last one, before the proxy stream starts.
- `config.proto`: `delay` becomes `delay_min` / `delay_max`; negative, reversed and duration-overflowing ranges are rejected at config load.
- `infra/conf`: parses the string delay; tests cover fixed values, ranges and invalid forms.

## Native frame padding (`ea2c7edc`, breaking)

The opaque format wrote a length field that includes its own varint. A vanilla server therefore split the stream one header short and had to take the protocol pipeline over — something a Fabric server mod cannot do without affecting ordinary players.

- One padding chunk becomes one or more configuration-state custom payload frames on `xmc:pad`; the length field now has the vanilla meaning (bytes after the field).
- Chunks above the 32767-byte serverbound payload limit are split; captured 2-byte turns send the smallest possible frame.
- Nothing reads padding any more: it is ordinary traffic that the next reader drops as an unknown packet. Both ends only send and apply the configured pauses.
- The first turn still counts the two Login Acknowledged bytes as its prefix; they are not repeated.
- `maxPacketDataLength` is raised from 32 KiB to 1 MiB (vanilla's clientbound custom payload limit), which a real configuration state can reach with registry data.

**Breaking:** both ends must run this version. No proto field was added for padding; the `paddings` length/direction semantics are unchanged, and `delay` moved from a number to a millisecond string.

Example:

```json
"paddings": [
  {"length": "44", "direction": "c2s", "delay": "0"},
  {"length": "64-128", "direction": "s2c", "delay": "100"},
  {"length": "25", "direction": "c2s", "delay": "50-150"},
  {"length": "32768-49152", "direction": "s2c"}
]
```

Both endpoints should still use the same array and the same `delay` ranges, because that is what reproduces the captured shape. Nothing is compared against the peer's schedule any more, though: the receiver does not consume padding, so a length, direction or turn-count difference can no longer fail or stall the handshake, it only changes what each side sends.

## Scope

Per the cleanup in #6769, this PR does **not** restore the XMC `README.md` / `*_test.go` files deleted in that squash commit. The only new test file is `padding_frames_test.go`, which covers the frame plan/reachability and the source of the padding stream, because the wire format changed here.

## Tests

```text
go test -count=1 ./infra/conf
go test -count=1 ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc
go build -o /tmp/xray-core-build ./main
go run ./infra/vformat -pwd . -mode check
go run ./infra/vprotogen -pwd . -mode check
```

## Validation fix

A legacy password longer than 113 bytes is now rejected when the configuration is built (`035c45de`), instead of being accepted and then failing every handshake: the verify token plus the password must fit one RSA-1024 PKCS#1 v1.5 block (128-11 bytes), so `rsa.EncryptPKCS1v15` was failing on the client and the server could not decrypt it either.

```text
go test -count=1 ./infra/conf ./transport/internet/finalmask/xmc
```

issues.title: Feature Request: Add udp+local:// DNS scheme (plain UDP local mode)
issues.body:
# Feature Request: Add `udp+local://` DNS scheme (plain UDP local mode)

## Summary

Xray's DNS configuration supports `+local` variants for HTTPS, h2c, QUIC and TCP, but there is **no `udp+local` scheme** for plain UDP DNS in local mode. This means there is currently **no way to send plain UDP DNS queries to a local resolver while bypassing the routing/dispatcher stack**.

## Current state

`app/dns/nameserver.go`, `NewServer()` switch (main branch):

```go
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "https"):      // DoH remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "h2c"):        // DoH h2c remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "https+local"): // DoH local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "h2c+local"):   // DoH h2c local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "quic+local"):  // DoQ local
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "tcp"):         // TCP remote
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "tcp+local"):   // TCP local
case strings.EqualFold(u.String(), "fakedns"):
```

Every protocol except plain UDP has a `+local` form. Plain UDP falls through to the default branch:

```go
if dest.Network == net.Network_UDP {
    return NewClassicNameServer(dest, dispatcher, ...)
}
```

Note that `NewClassicNameServer` receives the `dispatcher`, so plain UDP **always goes through the routing stack** — there is no way to bypass it.

## Why this matters (measured data)

For a local resolver (e.g. smartdns on `127.0.0.1`), bypassing the dispatcher matters. Measured on a local resolver over loopback, one A + one AAAA query for the same domain:

| Path | p50 | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `tcp+local://` (current workaround) | ~810µs | 2 TCP handshakes + 2 closes |
| `tcp+local://` pipelined on 1 conn | ~680µs | would need connection pooling, not implemented |
| **plain UDP, 2 packets sent in parallel** | **~376µs** | no handshake, no teardown |

The UDP path is ~2x faster than the current `tcp+local` workaround because it avoids TCP handshake/teardown entirely. Pairing responses by DNS ID worked in 200/200 trials with zero mismatch.

For users running a local caching resolver, this overhead is paid on every cache-miss lookup.

## Secondary issue: port parsing for bare `udp://` schemes

Related bug found while investigating. With:

```json
"dns": { "servers": ["udp://127.0.0.1:5353"] }
```

xray logs:

```
DNS: created UDP client initialized for udp://127.0.0.1:5353:53
```

The port becomes `5353:53` — the `:5353` is swallowed into the address (as a domain string) and then a default `:53` is appended by:

```go
// app/dns/nameserver_udp.go:41
if address.Port == 0 {
    address.Port = net.Port(53)
}
```

This is because `infra/conf/dns.go` builds the endpoint with `Address` and `Port` as separate fields, and `Address.Build()` calls `net.ParseAddress()` on the whole string including `:5353`, while `Port` stays 0.

Attempting `udp://127.0.0.1` (no port) resolves to `udp://127.0.0.1:53`, which happens to work, but the scheme is still parsed as a domain so the connection fails with:

```
failed to open connection to udp:udp://127.0.0.1:53
> too many colons in address
```

Contrast with `tcp+local`, which parses correctly because it uses `url.Hostname()` and `url.Port()` separately (`app/dns/nameserver_tcp.go:75-81`).

## Proposed change

Add a `udp+local` case that mirrors `tcp+local` — parse host/port via `url.Hostname()` / `url.Port()` and pass `nil` as the dispatcher:

```go
case strings.EqualFold(u.Scheme, "udp+local"): // DNS-over-UDP Local mode
    return NewUDPNameServer(u, nil, disableCache, serveStale, serveExpiredTTL, clientIP), nil
```

Where the new constructor resolves the destination the same way `baseTCPNameServer` does:

```go
port := net.Port(53)
if url.Port() != "" {
    if port, err = net.PortFromString(url.Port()); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
}
dest := net.UDPDestination(net.ParseAddress(url.Hostname()), port)
```

This would also give users a documented way to hit a local resolver on a non-53 port without the address-swallowing bug.

## Environment

issues.title: Feature request: configurable TLS fingerprint selection with weights and an explicit allowlist
issues.body:
As one of many VPN services using Xray, we’d find it useful to configure multiple TLS fingerprints, assign each a percentage (chance of choosing specific fingerprint on connection, analogous to `random`), and explicitly exclude fingerprints that do not work in our target networks. The core would select a fingerprint once per new connection according to those weights.

For example: **Firefox 9%, Chrome 70%, Edge 12%, Safari 9%**, with `ios`, `android`, and `chrome-133` excluded.

In our experience, Russian DPI blocks connections using those three fingerprints in some cases. Unrestricted random selection is therefore risky: individual connections may fail simply because an incompatible fingerprint was selected.

We previously used Firefox because it worked well in our environment. However, what works today may change, and having 100% of connections share the same normalized TLS fingerprint could itself help TSPU identify VPN traffic.

Weighted selection would reduce this uniformity, while explicit control over the allowed fingerprints would help preserve reliability. This would not make VPN traffic indistinguishable from browsers, but it would give operators a practical way to manage that tradeoff.

**The author of #7369 confirmed this independently:** they reproduced the 12288-byte threshold on v25.12.8, deployed a `ReshapeMultiBuffer` patch of the same shape on their relay (which was crashing about 100 times a day), and report interop unchanged against sing-box and Xray 24/25/26 over Reality, XHTTP and gRPC — https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/issues/7369#issuecomment-6991140613

#7424 came first and fixes the same panic at its source by not reading oversized hunks in the gRPC transport. Since `buf.NewExisted` is only called there, that removes the only producer of oversized buffers in the tree today.

This PR addresses the other half: `ReshapeMultiBuffer` assumes a single split is always enough and discards the `ErrBufferFull` that `Write` returns, so it silently truncates any buffer larger than `buf.Size` whatever produced it. I think the two are complementary rather than alternatives, but if you consider the producer-side fix sufficient I am happy to close this.

@RPRX, I rebased #7364 onto the requested `5e86165` and kept #5143’s direct `DispatchLink` path for ordinary VMess, including the removal of the post-authentication inbound timeout. I restored the upstream response codecs and command handling, so only two VMess files now differ from `main`.

<details>
<summary>Remaining changes on top of #5143</summary>

1. **`proxy/vmess/inbound/inbound.go` — `codecBody.ReadMultiBuffer`.** Keep the cancellation check after decoding. In the control run without it, the TCP destination received 144 bytes after cancellation. With the check, it received none.

3. **`proxy/vmess/inbound/inbound.go` — `Handler.Process`, `RequestCommandMux`.** Send incoming VMess Mux traffic to native `proxy/vless/multiplex`, with the VMess response header sent before the frames. Two processes built from the final source exchanged exact UDP replies from two distinct destinations through this path.

4. **`proxy/vmess/outbound/outbound.go` — command selection.** The existing three-line removal of the generic `v1.mux.cool` destination check remains. SingleXUDP still selects its command through the separate UDP path.

</details>

comments.issue_title: panic: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171] in XtlsPadding (VLESS outbound, Reality + Vision), recurring ~6x/hour on 25.6.8 / 25.9.5 / 25.12.8
comments.body:
Thank you @anonymousmeower, that explains it. We do have a gRPC inbound on this relay (7 clients, roughly a third of all connections), and the bursts line up with a threshold like 12288.

I reproduced it independently on v25.12.8 (`81f8f39`) with a small test: a 12288-byte buffer created with `buf.NewExisted` goes through `ReshapeMultiBuffer`, the second piece is exactly 8192 bytes, and `XtlsPadding` then computes `paddingLen = -21`. Agreed that clamping `paddingLen` is the wrong fix (it just trades a crash for truncation), the split has to be done properly.

This is what we run now on the production relay, in case it is useful as a starting point (it only changes the oversize path; buffers whose remainder fits are split exactly as before):

```go
tail := buffer1.BytesFrom(index)
var pieces []*buf.Buffer
for len(tail) > 0 {
	n := len(tail)
	if n > buf.Size-21 {
		n = buf.Size - 21
	}
	piece := buf.New()
	piece.Write(tail[:n])
	pieces = append(pieces, piece)
	tail = tail[n:]
}
buffer1.Resize(0, index)
mb2 = append(mb2, buffer1)
for _, piece := range pieces {
	mb2 = append(mb2, piece)
}
```

A test with sizes 8171 / 8192 / 8213 / 12288 / 16384 / 20000 / 40000 (with and without a TLS application-data header) passes: every piece is <= `buf.Size-21`, the concatenation equals the input, and `XtlsPadding` does not panic on any piece. The same test fails on the unpatched code at 12288. Interop with sing-box and Xray 24/25/26 clients over Reality, XHTTP and gRPC is unchanged in our matrix. We will report back after a few days of real traffic (the relay was crashing about 100 times a day before).

comments.body:
## 一句话结论

不做“进 Play 的强行伪装”，也不靠纯 pad 硬糊。**走“真协议 + 假节奏”**：登录和 Configuration 阶段按 MC 协议真走一遍（Client Info、Known Packs、Registry、Tags、Finish），客户端**不回最后的确认包**，于是停在 Configuration——不建玩家、不发区块。缺的两样东西用 pad 补：进服的体量、之后的 20 次/秒心跳。真客户端如果把确认包回了，就按 vanilla 原来的位置（白名单检查处）把它踢掉。

## 抓包（26.3，第三方登录，加密）

| 状态 | 客户端→服务端 | 服务端→客户端 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 站着不动 | 21 包/秒，89 B/s | 41 包/秒，5.6 KB/s |
| 转视角 | 35 包/秒，267 B/s | 42 包/秒，6 KB/s |
| 跑动 | 43 包/秒，697 B/s | 99 包/秒，69 KB/s |
| 进服加载 | 43 包/秒（含 20/秒的小回执） | 2.2 MB / 12 秒 |

- 心跳间隔中位 50.0 ms，很稳；加载卡顿时出现过 4.7 秒完全没有上行。
- 开压缩后真机心跳只有 **3 字节**；`xmc:pad` 帧是 11 字节（7 字符通道）或 7 字节（3 字符通道），包数能对上，字节多一点点。
- 下行大头是 1400 字节的 TCP 段，所以“大流量”在链路上天然像区块下载——这点对我们有利。

## 第三方登录

- #7416 已经就绪且测过，目前未发现问题。

## 通道名

- 通道名必须可配：固定名字对有账号的探测者是特征；而且名字长度直接决定 pad 帧长度（7 字符 11 字节 / 3 字符 7 字节）。

---

comments.issue_title: XMC finalmask: Bound padding schedules; Fix delay placement; Stop compressing frames
comments.body:
@RPRX 结论先说：MC 协议本身没有 padding，也没有任何"延迟/时序"字段；真机上 join 收尾的最后一个包之后也没有停顿——同一个 tick 里就会发 `Client Tick End`，之后每 50 ms 一个。所以"the last one 之后需不需要 delay"在真机上对应的是"下一个包在同一个 tick 内到"，而不是"停一下"。

**MC 协议到底是什么**

1. 帧：一条 TCP 连接上就是 VarInt 长度分帧，`长度 | 包体`；包体是 `packet id + 字段`。`Set Compression` 之后包体前面多一个 `data length`：`data length = 0` 表示未压缩，非 0 才走 zlib。vanilla 服务端接受超过 threshold 的未压缩包，只拒绝小于 threshold 的压缩包（这个 PR 第 4 点靠的就是它）。帧上限 2^21-1；serverbound custom payload 数据 ≤ 32767 B，clientbound ≤ 1 MiB。
2. 状态机：Handshaking → Status / Login → Configuration → Play。登录阶段可选 RSA + AES-CFB8；之后整条流（包括长度字段）都是密文，路径上的观察者只看得到"什么时候、多少字节"。
3. 协议里唯一和时间有关的规则是 keep-alive：服务端每 1–15 s 发一次，客户端 15 s 不回被踢，20 s 收不到就 Timed out。除此之外没有节流、没有填充、没有时序协商。
4. 客户端的"节奏"是 20 Hz 游戏循环（50 ms/tick）：一个 tick 里产生的包各自 write+flush，Nagle 关掉，所以 wire 上的间隔基本就是 tick。

**"最后一个包之后"在真机上**

查了 26.1 官方客户端（反编译），`Minecraft.tick()` 里的顺序是：

- `gameMode.tick()` → `Connection.tick()` → `ClientPacketListener.tick()` → `notifyPlayerLoaded()`：加载地形结束时发 `Player Loaded`；
- `level.tickEntities()`：玩家第一次 tick（wiki 说"第一次玩家 tick 发生在这个包和下一个 Client Tick End 之间"就是这里）；
- `connection.send(ServerboundClientTickEndPacket.INSTANCE)`：`Client Tick End`，无字段，2 字节帧。

所以 `Player Loaded` 和下一个 `Client Tick End` 在同一个 tick 内，间隔就是该 tick 剩下的工作量（通常几 ms），然后才是 50 ms 网格。capture 看起来"停在最后"，是因为 schedule 只建模到 player_loaded，后面交给隧道了；真机在后面是持续的心跳。

**对 #7423**

- "pause 前移到 turn 上、最后一个 turn 之后不暂停"是对的：captured gap 属于"下一个包什么时候来"，不属于"上一个包之后停多久"；最后一个 turn 后面没有下一个 turn，这个 pause 没有地方放。
- 硬加一个尾部 delay 反而会造出真机没有的空洞：真机那个位置只有 tick 的剩余时间（几 ms）。
- join 收尾之后真正缺的不是 delay，而是 20 Hz 心跳；而 XMC 停在 Configuration，这个状态里 vanilla 客户端只有回应、没有 tick 包，所以它也不是 padding schedule 能补的，属于另一个设计问题。

结论：这个 PR 不需要为"最后一个之后的 delay"改模型。


参考：[Packets#Packet_format](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Packet_format)、[FAQ 登录序列](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/FAQ#What's_the_normal_login_sequence_for_a_client?)、[Player Loaded](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Player_Loaded)、[Keep Alive](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Keep_Alive_(clientbound))

Additional end-to-end observation: cancelling HTTP requests while the VPN client stayed running led to the same quota deduction as a full download in a controlled WaterWall → Xray/XMPlus test.

Each run requested 40 HTTPS objects of 2 MiB each (two parallel requests per simulated video, 20 videos). The full run completed all 40. The cancellation run cancelled each pair 300 ms after both HTTP requests were sent, without stopping the VPN client. The controlled origin completed its writes for all 40 objects in both runs.

| Run | Reported downlink (bytes) | VLESS payload read by client (bytes) | Reported uplink (bytes) | Actual quota deduction (bytes) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Full | 84,080,320 | 84,080,320 | 29,110 | 84,109,430 |
| Cancelled | 84,080,320 | 6,565,384 | 29,110 | 84,109,430 |

The cancelled run's downlink-to-client gap was **77,514,936 bytes (73.92 MiB)**. At a traffic multiplier of 1, the new panel traffic rows reconciled exactly with the actual quota decrease. This experiment measures the total gap between server reporting and client reads. It did not isolate failed writes from bytes accepted by intermediate buffers. The impact on customers who reported unexpected quota use is still unknown.

> ~是仅 panic 而不会通过认证吧~

Yes, you're correct — it only causes a panic and does **not** bypass authentication.

After reviewing the code and running tests, here's the precise breakdown:

**Root cause — `proxy/socks/protocol.go` line 206:**

```go
// If s.config.Address is set to a domain (e.g. "localhost" or "example.com"),
// AsAddress() returns a domainAddress, and calling .IP() on it panics.
udpHub, err := internet.ListenSystemPacket(
    context.Background(),
    &net.UDPAddr{IP: responseAddress.IP(), Port: 0},  // 💥 panic here
    nil,
)
```

This is because `domainAddress.IP()` in `common/net/address.go` unconditionally panics:

```go
func (domainAddress) IP() net.IP {
    panic("Calling IP() on a DomainAddress.")
}
```

**Why it is NOT an authentication bypass:**

The panic occurs at line 206, which is reached only *after* `auth5()` completes successfully at line 148. An unauthenticated or wrongly-authenticated client is rejected before the panic site is ever reached (confirmed by testing all three scenarios: no-auth client, wrong-password client, and no-auth server).

**Trigger conditions:**

The vulnerable path requires the server operator to have explicitly set `address` to a domain name (e.g. `"localhost"`) in the SOCKS inbound config. A remote attacker has no control over `responseAddress` — it comes from `s.config.Address` (server config), not from client input. The client only needs to send a `UDP ASSOCIATE` command to trigger the crash once the misconfiguration is in place.

**Impact:** This is a **misconfiguration-induced crash** (DoS), not a security vulnerability. If `address` is left empty (default) or set to a valid IP, the panic never occurs.

**Describe the bug**
If the AmneziaVPN app is force-quit while an XRay (VLESS) connection is active, the service keeps the XRay engine and its `tun2socks` child running indefinitely. On my Mac they stayed alive for 7 days while I later used AmneziaWG; the service grew to 1462 threads and 751 MB (peak 1.2 GB). I force-quit the app from the Dock because it takes long to close.

**To Reproduce**
1. Amnezia Premium on macOS, connect via VLESS/XRay.
2. Force-quit AmneziaVPN (Dock → Force Quit).
3. `pgrep -fl tun2socks` — still running; `ifconfig utun22` — still up. Reopen the app and connect via AmneziaWG: the old `tun2socks`/XRay engine remain.

(Steps reconstructed from what happened on my machine plus the code below; normal protocol switching in a running app cleans up correctly.)

**Expected behavior**
When the client disconnects or dies, the service stops the processes and the XRay engine it started for that client.

**Observed (stack sample instead of logs)**
- `tun2socks` started by the service on Nov 12, still alive on Nov 19 with `utun22` up while AmneziaWG was connected.
- `sudo sample AmneziaVPN-service 3`: 1456 of 1462 threads are idle Go runtime threads of the embedded XRay library (`runtime.asmcgocall → runtime.pthread_cond_wait_trampoline`). Go does not return OS threads, so they stay until the service restarts.
- `launchctl kickstart -k system/AmneziaVPN-service`: threads 1463 → 17, memory 751 → 105 MB, orphaned tun2socks gone.

**Where it seems to come from**
1. `IpcServer::createPrivilegedProcess()` (`ipc/ipcserver.cpp`) inserts every process into `m_processes` and never removes it; nothing stops privileged processes or calls `Xray::stopAny()` when the client goes away.

3. Not verified: on macOS each concurrent DNS lookup through libSystem occupies an OS thread; `PreferGo` / `GODEBUG=netdns=go` might reduce spikes.

Also noticed: the app takes long to quit on macOS, which pushes users to force-quit.

**Desktop:** macOS 27.0.1 (Apple Silicon), AmneziaVPN 5.1.0 (5.1.0.6)
**Server:** Amnezia Premium (Luxembourg); app split tunnelling enabled

issues.title: Windows: Full-tunnel route capture overrides connected routes on other interfaces
issues.body:
## Description

In Windows full-tunnel mode (VpnAllSites), AmneziaVPN clones routes from other network interfaces onto the VPN interface. This includes directly connected networks used by virtual networking systems such as Windows HNS.

The cloned routes can override the original routes, causing Windows to send traffic to local networks through the VPN interface instead of the interface that owns those networks. This breaks connectivity to HNS container networks, including return traffic.

## Environment
- AmneziaVPN 5.1.0.6
- Windows
- Full-tunnel mode (VpnAllSites)
- Split tunneling disabled
- Windows HNS NAT container network

## Steps to reproduce
1. Create and start a Windows HNS NAT container network.
2. Verify the connected route to the HNS subnet through the HNS virtual Ethernet interface.
3. Connect AmneziaVPN in full-tunnel mode with split tunneling disabled.
4. Inspect the IPv4 routing table and run Find-NetRoute for an address in the HNS subnet.

## Observed behavior
The same route 10.250.0.0/24 is present on two interfaces:
- AmneziaVPN, ifIndex 30, metric 0.
- HNS vEthernet NAT, ifIndex 96, metric 256.

Find-NetRoute selects the AmneziaVPN interface instead of HNS for destinations in this subnet.

The same behavior was observed for other connected networks: 172.26.144.0/20, 192.168.56.0/24, and 192.168.88.0/24.

This can cause traffic destined for local virtual networks to be sent through the VPN interface, breaking container connectivity.

## Expected behavior
Full-tunnel route capture should preserve routes to directly connected networks on other interfaces. Traffic destined for an HNS container network should continue to use the HNS interface, while Internet-bound traffic continues to use the VPN.

## Relevant implementation
In WindowsRouteMonitor::updateCapturedRoutes() in windowsroutemonitor.cpp, eligible routes are cloned onto the VPN interface. The observed behavior suggests that connected routes belonging to other interfaces are not excluded.

WireguardUtilsWindows::updateRoutePrefix() enables default-route capture when a 0.0.0.0/0 route is installed.

This behavior was reproduced with split tunneling disabled, so it is not limited to the split-tunneling scenario in issue #2830.

Related issue: https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/issues/2830

issues.title: Ubuntu 24.04: DNS not configured on amn0 after connect (race condition with systemd-resolved restart)
issues.body:
**Environment**
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- AmneziaVPN: 4.8.15.4
- Protocol: AmneziaWG2

**Problem**
After connecting, the VPN tunnel is up but internet doesn't work.
- `ping 8.8.8.8` succeeds (tunnel is alive)
- `ping google.com` hangs (DNS broken)
- `resolvectl status` hangs with `Connection timed out`
- `resolvectl status amn0` shows `Current Scopes: none` instead of `DNS`

Happens on most connects, especially noticeable right after the first connection attempt.

**Root cause**
AmneziaVPN restarts `systemd-resolved` and immediately tries to configure DNS on amn0 via DBus. The service hasn't fully initialized its DBus interface yet, so the call fails silently and DNS is never set on amn0.

Visible in `/var/log/AmneziaVPN/AmneziaVPN-service.log` right after connect:
```
[DEBUG] Amnezia  : Restarting systemd-resolved.service
[DEBUG] Amnezia  : Flush dns completed
[ERROR] Amnezia DnsUtilsLinux : Error retrieving the DNS domains from the DBus service
[ERROR] Amnezia DnsUtilsLinux : Error received from the DBus service
[ERROR] Amnezia DnsUtilsLinux : Error received from the DBus service
```

**Workaround**
Note: `systemctl restart systemd-resolved` hangs when resolved is stuck — use `kill` + `start` instead.

Manual fix (run after connecting when DNS doesn't work):
```bash
sudo systemctl kill systemd-resolved
sudo systemctl start systemd-resolved

for i in $(seq 1 15); do
    busctl status org.freedesktop.resolve1 &>/dev/null && break
    sleep 1
done

sudo resolvectl dns amn0 8.8.8.8 1.0.0.1
sudo resolvectl domain amn0 "~."
```

Permanent automated fix — udev rule that triggers a systemd service on amn0 creation:

`/etc/udev/rules.d/99-amnezia-dns.rules`:
```
ACTION=="add", SUBSYSTEM=="net", KERNEL=="amn0", TAG+="systemd", ENV{SYSTEMD_WANTS}="amnezia-fix-dns.service"
```

`/etc/systemd/system/amnezia-fix-dns.service`:
```ini
[Unit]
Description=Fix AmneziaVPN DNS on amn0
After=systemd-resolved.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/amnezia-fix-dns.sh
```

`/usr/local/bin/amnezia-fix-dns.sh`:
```bash
#!/bin/bash
for i in $(seq 1 15); do
    busctl status org.freedesktop.resolve1 &>/dev/null && break
    sleep 1
done
resolvectl dns amn0 8.8.8.8 1.0.0.1
resolvectl domain amn0 "~."
```

**Expected behavior**
DNS should be correctly configured on amn0 immediately after connecting.

AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.1 (AWG 3.1), Android 16, OnePlus 15.
Self-hosted AmneziaWG, mobile network (Russia), battery set
to "Unrestricted" for AmneziaVPN.

Problem
After the phone has been idle with the screen off, the tunnel
sometimes stalls: nothing works (Telegram, browser) until I
manually disconnect and reconnect in AmneziaVPN. It happens
several times a day. A manual reconnect always fixes it
immediately.

What we see on the server side
We captured traffic on our server during these episodes. While
the tunnel is stalled, no packets from the phone reach the server
at all — no handshake initiation, nothing, for 4–44 minutes.
Other devices on the same server work normally at the same time.
Typical sequence: the phone wakes up, sends a few data packets
with the old session from a new NAT port (the mobile operator
changed it during sleep), the server drops them (keys older than
180 s), and then the phone never sends a new handshake. A manual
reconnect opens a new socket, the handshake completes in ~0.1 s,
and traffic flows right away.

An option to detect a stalled tunnel and restart it automatically,
for example:
- if the latest handshake is older than ~140 s

  wireguard-tools reresolve-dns) while the app has traffic to send,
  or
- if a periodic check through the tunnel (ping/HTTP) fails
  N times in a row,
then recreate the socket and re-handshake — the same as a manual
reconnect. Configurable interval and on/off switch.

Similar features exist in other clients: WG Tunnel ("Restart
tunnel on ping failure"), mihomo-based clients (fallback groups
with health checks).

Server-side keepalive does not help here: we tried
PersistentKeepalive 25 on the server for this peer — the server
cannot reach the phone after the operator's NAT mapping changes,
only the phone can recover by sending first.

Thank you for AmneziaVPN!

Deadlock between AmneziaVPN-service and kernel network locks on lid close (macOS 26.6, app 5.0.0.5, VLESS) — configd killed by WATCHDOG
issues.body:
## Summary

On macOS 26.6 (25G72), closing the MacBook lid while the VPN is connected reliably
deadlocks the system networking stack. A kernel lock cycle forms between
`AmneziaVPN-service` and the kernel, `configd`'s `IPConfigurationAgentQueue` stalls,
and after 60 seconds the watchdog terminates `configd`.

This happens every single day, on every lid close with the VPN running.

## Environment

- AmneziaVPN for macOS **5.0.0.5**
- macOS 26.6 (build 25G72)
- MacBookPro18,3 (Apple Silicon)
- Protocol: **VLESS (XRay)**
- `tun2socks` is present in the process list (41 threads), consistent with the
  XRay/VLESS userspace tunnel path
- Report incident ID: 19D61D4C-C90C-4BF8-AE79-91B9C65CAC96
- Report type: bug_type 409 (WATCHDOG stackshot), `displayState: OFF`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Connect the VPN.
2. Close the MacBook lid.
3. Within ~60 seconds a `configd` watchdog report is generated.

## Actual result

`configd` is killed by the [watchdog]

## Root cause from the stackshot — four-way lock cycle

1. `configd` thread 103010 (`IPConfigurationAgentQueue`) waits on kernel mutex
   `0xfffffe000c571830`, owned by kernel thread 103456 (`thread call high #27`).
2. Kernel thread 103456 waits on krwlock `0xfffffe000c5a4270` **for reading**,
   owned by thread 104354.
3. Thread 104354 belongs to **AmneziaVPN-service (pid 553)** and waits on kernel
   mutex `0x5162d882b476c1c1`, owned by kernel thread 5256.
4. Kernel thread 5256 waits on mutex `0xfffffe000c571830` — back to 103456.

The cycle never breaks, so the whole networking subsystem stalls.

## Additional observations

- `AmneziaVPN-service` had **259 threads** and **~955 MB** resident memory, with
  ~592k page faults. Roughly 200 of those threads were parked on the same
  `0xfffffe000c571830` mutex, and about a dozen more on the krwlock held by 104354.
  The thread and memory growth looks like a leak independent of the deadlock.
- `tun2socks` (41 threads) is blocked on the same mutex.
- The `AmneziaVPN` GUI process is also stuck: thread 16371 waits on krwlock
  `0xfffffe000c5a4270` for writing, owned by 104354.

## Likely trigger

On lid close macOS tears down Wi-Fi and reconfigures interfaces, so `configd`
dismantles network services while the client simultaneously tears down its `utun`.
The two sides appear to acquire the network locks in opposite order.

## Workaround

Disconnecting the VPN before closing the lid avoids the issue entirely.

## Attachment

Full watchdog stackshot attached.

[Error.rtf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30687946/Error.rtf)

The desktop GUI client crashes with `EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV)` about 30 seconds after the Mac wakes from sleep, while auto-reconnecting an Xray/VLESS connection. Full macOS crash report attached.

Crashing thread is the `VpnConnection` worker thread:

```
Exception Type: EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV)
KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS at 0x0000000000000430

Thread 3 Crashed:: QThread
0   QtCore       0x1062f6e5c 0x10620c000 + 962140
1   AmneziaVPN   VpnProtocol::connectionStateChanged(Vpn::ConnectionState) + 60
2   AmneziaVPN   VpnProtocol::setConnectionState(Vpn::ConnectionState) + 656
3   AmneziaVPN   XrayProtocol::stop() + 1844
4   AmneziaVPN   VpnConnection::reconnectToVpn() + 244
5   QtCore       QObject::event(QEvent*) + 672
6   QtCore       QCoreApplicationPrivate::sendPostedEvents(...)
```

**Possible cause**

Reading the 5.0.1.5 sources, the crash looks like the `emit connectionStateChanged(...)` on the last line of `XrayProtocol::stop()` running on an object that is no longer alive:

- `wakeup` and `networkChanged` are connected to `VpnConnection::reconnectToVpn` in `createProtocolConnections()` (`client/vpnConnection.cpp:387-390`). That method runs on every connect and never disconnects the previous connections, so the number of queued `reconnectToVpn` invocations per single wake-up grows with each connect/disconnect cycle in a session.
- `XrayProtocol::stop()` (`client/core/protocols/xrayProtocol.cpp:119-166`) makes five synchronous IPC calls with `waitForFinished()`, each spinning a nested event loop — so those extra queued `reconnectToVpn` events get delivered while `stop()` is still on the stack.
- Re-entering the reconnect path resets/replaces `m_vpnProtocol`, so `setConnectionState(Disconnected)` at the end of `stop()` fires on a freed object.

This may be the client-side counterpart of #2637, which describes the same kind of race in AmneziaVPN-service.

**To Reproduce**

Approximate — the exact number of connect/disconnect cycles before the crash isn't known:

1. Connect with Xray/VLESS on macOS
2. Leave the VPN connected and let the Mac sleep (close the lid)
3. Wake it up
4. The app crashes within ~30 s

**Expected behavior**

The client reconnects after wake without crashing.

**Log files**

`report.txt` attached (full macOS crash report). The app had been running 1 h 34 min; `Time Since Wake: 30 seconds` at the moment of the crash.

**Desktop:**
- OS: macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), Apple M2 Pro (Mac14,9), arm64
- Version: 5.0.1.5, installed as .pkg, Qt 6.10
- Protocol: Xray / VLESS

**Additional context**

I'm not a developer — the crash report is genuine, but the stack-trace analysis above was done with an AI assistant against the 5.0.1.5 sources, so please treat that part as a hypothesis rather than a verified diagnosis.

issues.title: fix(vpn): keep the protocol alive while a service call waits
issues.body:
Fixes #3042.

Related: #2933 and the reports in it describe the kernel-level deadlock around `tun2socks`/`utun` on macOS; this change does not address that, only the use-after-free in the client.

## Problem

On macOS (AmneziaVPN 5.1.0, macOS 26.2, Xray protocol) the app crashes after the Mac sleeps and the Wi-Fi network changes, while the VPN is reconnecting. Two crash reports, symbols only:

- `SIGSEGV`: `VpnConnection::reconnectToVpn` → `XrayProtocol::stop` → `VpnProtocol::setConnectionState` → `VpnProtocol::connectionStateChanged` (the fault is inside the signal emission)
- `SIGBUS`: `VpnConnection::connectToVpn` → `XrayProtocol::start` → `XrayProtocol::startTun2Socks` → `QString::arg` (copying a garbage `QString` member)

Both look like a freed `XrayProtocol` that is still used.

## Cause

`QRemoteObjectPendingCall::waitForFinished()` runs a nested `QEventLoop` ([qremoteobjectreplica.cpp](https://github.com/qt/qtremoteobjects/blob/dev/src/remoteobjects/qremoteobjectreplica.cpp), `QConnectedReplicaImplementation::waitForFinished`). `stop()` and `start()` make several such calls, so while they wait, queued slots of `VpnConnection` run on the same thread: `disconnectFromVpn`, `connectToVpn` and another `reconnectToVpn` (the service emits `networkChanged` and `wakeup` together after wake). `disconnectFromVpn` and `connectToVpn` drop the last reference to `m_vpnProtocol`, the protocol is destroyed, and `stop()`/`start()` go on using it when the nested loop returns.

## Change

`reconnectToVpn`, `connectToVpn` and `disconnectFromVpn` keep their own reference to the protocol for the duration of the call. After `stop()`/`start()` they check that `m_vpnProtocol` is still the same object and otherwise leave the new state alone (no restart of a protocol that was replaced, no reset of a newer connection).

## Verification

- A small model with real Qt: a protocol whose `stop()` runs a nested event loop in which the owner drops its pointer, built with AddressSanitizer. The current pattern gives `heap-use-after-free` in `stop()`; the pattern from this change runs clean.
- `git clang-format` reports nothing on the changed lines.
- Not done: the full client was not built or run, and the sleep + network change scenario was not reproduced end to end. The change is small, but please test it on a Mac if you can.

## Not covered

If `disconnectFromVpn` runs while `XrayProtocol::start()` waits for the service, `start()` still goes on to start tun2socks afterwards. That is a separate change in `xrayProtocol.cpp`.

**Describe the bug**

AmneziaVPN 5.0.1.5 on macOS and Windows ignores the configured custom SSH port and always tries to connect to port 22, resulting in error 305 (Timeout).

The same VPS connects successfully from Android using the same custom SSH port and ED25519 SSH key.

**To Reproduce**

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Configure a VPS with SSH listening on a non-standard port (e.g. 22222).
2. Configure SSH authentication using an ED25519 key.
3. Add the VPS to AmneziaVPN using the custom SSH port.
4. Try to connect from macOS or Windows.
5. AmneziaVPN fails with error 305 (Timeout).
6. Check the VPS with `tcpdump` and observe connection attempts to port 22 instead of the configured SSH port.

**Expected behavior**

AmneziaVPN should connect to the SSH port specified in the server configuration.

**Log files**

No relevant SSH connection attempts from the desktop clients appear in the server logs when SSH is not available on port 22.

**Screenshots**

Not applicable.

**Desktop:**

* OS: macOS 26.6.2 / Windows 25H2
* Version: AmneziaVPN 5.0.1.5
* SSH authentication: ED25519 key

**Smartphone:**

* Device: Android smartphone
* OS: Android 16
* Version: AmneziaVPN 5.0.1.5
* SSH authentication: ED25519 key

**Server:**

* OS: Ubuntu 24.04
* SSH port: Custom non-standard port

**Additional context**

SSH access to the VPS works normally from both macOS and Windows using the standard SSH client, custom SSH port, and ED25519 key.

However, AmneziaVPN 5.0.1.5 on macOS and Windows ignores the configured SSH port and attempts to connect to port 22 instead.

AmneziaVPN 5.0.1.5 on Android works correctly with the same VPS, custom SSH port, and ED25519 key.

As a workaround, opening SSH on port 22 allows the desktop clients to connect successfully.

issues.title: Windows 11 24H2, 5.1.0.6: desktop client exits on Disconnect — looks like a race between Xray stop and the service channel
issues.body:
Приветствую.

Прежде всего — спасибо за клиент и за то, что проект открыт: разбираться по исходникам и по вашим ответам в обращениях можно, и это очень помогает.

Пишу о поведении, которое мешает в работе, и постараюсь изложить его так, чтобы вам было меньше работы: только наблюдения, журналы и то, что я уже проверил сам.

**Что происходит**

Нажимаю "Отключить". В части случаев всё проходит как надо: значок остаётся в трее, служба убирает маршруты. В остальных случаях окно и значок исчезают — программа завершается, а служба продолжает работать. Подключение при этом всегда проходит нормально.

Частота. За шесть циклов "подключить — отключить" подряд: четыре завершения. После того как в раздельное туннелирование по приложениям были добавлены две программы, из двух циклов завершился один. Похоже, дело не в настройках, а в моменте — то есть в гонке.

**Обстановка**

- Windows 11 IoT Enterprise LTSC, 10.0.26100 (24H2), x64.
- AmneziaVPN 5.1.0.6 (файл `C:\Program Files\AmneziaVPN\AmneziaVPN.exe`), Qt 6.11.1 (`Qt6RemoteObjects.dll` 6.11.1.0).
- Драйвер `mullvad-split-tunnel.sys` 1.2.5.0, служба `AmneziaVPNSplitTunnel`.
- Протокол VLESS (XRay) с `tun2socks.exe`.
- Настройки: раздельное туннелирование по сайтам включено; по приложениям включено, в списке две записи (`max.exe`, `max-service.exe`); kill switch выключен; собственный DNS Amnezia выключен; автозапуск с ключом `--autostart`, запуск свёрнутым.
- Клиент запущен обычным путём (автозапуск и оболочка рабочего стола), внешним менеджером процессов не управляется.

**Что видно в журнале службы**

Удачный цикл — служба успевает всё сделать, канал жив:

```
[16:48:11.724Z] Xray::stopXray()
[16:48:13.443Z] IpcServerProcess errorOccurred  QProcess::Crashed
[16:48:13.457Z] RouterWin::clearSavedRoutes forward rows size: 8
[16:48:13.460Z] Router::clearSavedRoutes : removed routes: 4 of 8
```

Неудачный цикл — те же шаги, но после остановки `tun2socks` служба замолкает, уборки маршрутов нет:

```
[16:48:53.761Z] Xray::stopXray()
[16:48:55.561Z] IpcServerProcess errorOccurred  QProcess::Crashed
```

Ранний неудачный цикл, где ошибка канала видна явно:

```
[15:40:11.985Z] Xray::stopXray()
[15:40:12.424Z] QWindowsPipeWriter: write failed. (Канал был закрыт.)
[15:40:13.729Z] IpcServerProcess errorOccurred  QProcess::Crashed
```

Между командой отключения и обрывом канала проходит от 0.4 до 1.7 секунды. В удачных циклах `clearSavedRoutes` успевает выполниться, в неудачных — нет.

**Что я проверил сам, чтобы не отнимать ваше время**

1. **Падения нет.** В журнале Application за день нет ни одного события 1000 или 1001 по `AmneziaVPN.exe` в моменты этих циклов. Завершение тихое — поэтому и обратился, а не отправил отчёт о сбое.
2. **Драйвер раздельного туннелирования, судя по всему, здесь ни при чём.** Пока список исключённых приложений был пуст, в журнале на каждом цикле повторялось `Stopping Split tunnel not successfull`. После добавления двух программ появились `Set Process Config ok`, `Driver is ready`, `New Network Config Applied`, `Pushing new Ruleset for Split-Tunnel`, и эта строка из новых циклов исчезла. Поведение при отключении, однако, не изменилось. Спасибо за разбор в #3216: по нему стало понятно, что пустой список ведёт себя как выключенное раздельное туннелирование.
3. **Накопленное состояние службы тоже не объясняет.** Остановка и запуск `AmneziaVPN-service` сбрасывают состояние драйвера, а исход при отключении остаётся прежним.
4. **Сеть и сервер в порядке.** Подключение проходит, трафик идёт, DNS отвечает; от длительности сеанса исход не зависит.

**Предположение**

Похоже на гонку между остановкой Xray с завершением `tun2socks` и разрывом канала между интерфейсом и службой. В неудачном варианте интерфейс закрывает соединение раньше, чем служба доходит до отправки финального состояния и до `clearSavedRoutes`: служба остаётся с невыполненной уборкой, интерфейс — завершённым. Если предположение неверно, поправьте, пожалуйста.

**Отдельно, возможно тот же корень**

issues.title: feat(split-tunneling): wildcard site entries, resolved by observing DNS
issues.body:
Fixes #1607.

## Why a wildcard cannot simply be added to the list

Site split tunnelling selects by destination address, because that is all a
routing table has. The addresses behind `*.discord.gg` are not knowable when the
entry is typed, and a CDN keeps changing them, so there is nothing to install.
Entering a domain already works by resolving it once and storing the answer, but
a wildcard cannot be resolved at all: there is no query that returns every name
below a label.

The only place where the name still exists is the DNS exchange itself. This
change puts a forwarder where the system already sends its queries, relays them
to the real resolvers, and installs an exclusion route for the addresses of the
answers whose name matches a pattern, while the answer is still on its way back
to the application.

## What is in it

Four commits, each one reviewable on its own:

1. **The forwarder, the shared definition of a wildcard, and the route table.**
   No caller yet.
2. **The UI and configuration path**: storing a pattern, and carrying it to the
   daemon.
3. **The daemon and the platform work**: installing, permitting and withdrawing
   what is learned.
4. **Fixes from the review** below: reserved addresses, the server switch, route
   lifetime, per-pattern budgets, dedicated firewall anchors on Linux and macOS,
   UDP/TCP failover in the forwarder, client-side gating and log privacy.

### Trusting an answer

What the forwarder reports becomes a route in a privileged daemon, so a reply is
believed only when all of this holds: it arrived from the resolver the query was
sent to, on a socket connected to it; the transaction id and the question match
the query; the response bit is set, the opcode is zero, there is no error, and
the answer is not truncated. Addresses are taken only from records whose owner is
the queried name or a name reached from it through the CNAMEs of that same
message, and each address inherits the shortest TTL along that path. Everything
else is handed to the application untouched and reported to nobody.

Because the forwarder replaces the system's resolver list, it does the
failover the system would otherwise do. A UDP query is retransmitted across
the configured resolvers (1 s per attempt, 5 s in total, a single resolver
being retried), a late answer to an earlier attempt is still accepted, and the
resolver that answered last is tried first. A TCP resolver that closes with
queries outstanding is reconnected and the queries resent. Only when the budget
runs out is the query answered with SERVFAIL, rather than left to time out.

Queries are served from the machine itself and from directly attached
subnets of other interfaces (local containers). Peers reaching the address
over the tunnel are refused, because what the forwarder learns becomes a
route.

### Names are never flattened

A DNS label may legally contain a dot. Names coming off the wire are kept as a
list of labels and compared label by label, so a single label whose bytes read
`x.example.com` does not pass for a name below `example.com`. Patterns are stored
canonically: lower case, no trailing dot, the base put through IDNA, and a path,
white space or an empty label refused at the point of entry. `*.пример.рф` is
stored as `*.xn--e1afmkfd.xn--p1ai`, which is the form that actually arrives.

### How long a learned route lives

A learned route lasts for the session. It is not withdrawn on a timer: an open
connection keeps using the address after the TTL, and the system resolver can
serve the record from its cache for as long as the TTL says. Once the full TTL
plus an hour has passed (on a monotonic clock), the entry is stale. A stale
entry is evicted, least recently seen first, only when its pattern or the
table is full. All learned routes are withdrawn on disconnect, on a server
switch to a different configuration, and when the pattern list changes.

[macOS] App hangs on launch (100% CPU, no window, only tray icon) when displays are mirrored
issues.body:
## Description
After updating to 5.1.1.9, the app no longer opens its main window on macOS. Only the tray icon appears and the main thread spins at 100% CPU. Disconnecting the external monitor fixes it immediately — the app launches normally.

## Environment
- AmneziaVPN: 5.1.1 (9), `AmneziaVPN_5.1.1.9_macos_x64.pkg`
- macOS: 14.7.2 Sonoma (23H311)
- Hardware: MacBook Pro M2 (Mac14,7), 8 GB
- Displays (mirror mode):
  - Built-in Retina: 2560×1600 (scale 2×)
  - Samsung Odyssey G91SD: 5120×1440 (32:9, scale 1×) — set as Main

## Steps to reproduce
1. Connect an external monitor with a different aspect ratio/scale factor than the built-in display.
2. Enable display mirroring.
3. Launch AmneziaVPN.

## Expected behavior
Main window opens.

## Actual behavior
- Only the tray icon is shown, the window never appears.
- The `AmneziaVPN` main thread is stuck in a busy loop (~100% CPU) — macOS spindump reports a hang.
- `AmneziaVPN-service` is running normally (idle in its event loop).
- After disconnecting the external monitor, the app starts normally.

## Spindump excerpt
Main thread is spinning at the same address for all 79 samples (7.85s):

    Thread 0x115fe  DispatchQueue "com.apple.main-thread"  79 samples  cpu time 7.770s
      ??? (AmneziaVPN + 2828644) [0x10120a964] 1-79

Full spindump attached.

## Possible cause
Probably a Qt window geometry / devicePixelRatio recalculation loop when the window is restored on a mirrored screen whose scale factor differs between the physical displays (2× vs 1×).

## Workaround
Launch the app before connecting the external monitor, or use extended desktop mode instead of mirroring.

comments.issue_title: [macOS] Client crashes (SIGSEGV) on auto-reconnect after wake from sleep with Xray — 5.0.1.5
comments.body:
The crash in this report is addressed by #3494.

The stack matches the one here (`VpnConnection::reconnectToVpn` → `XrayProtocol::stop` → `VpnProtocol::setConnectionState` → `connectionStateChanged`, SIGSEGV), and the diagnosis in the description is right: `QRemoteObjectPendingCall::waitForFinished()` runs a nested `QEventLoop`, so while `stop()` waits for the service, queued `disconnectFromVpn`, `connectToVpn` or another `reconnectToVpn` run and drop the last reference to `m_vpnProtocol`. `stop()` then goes on using the freed protocol. The same thing shows up on 5.1.0 as a SIGBUS in `connectToVpn` → `XrayProtocol::start` → `startTun2Socks` → `QString::arg`.

#3494 keeps a reference to the protocol for the duration of `reconnectToVpn`, `connectToVpn` and `disconnectFromVpn` and checks that it was not replaced meanwhile. A small Qt model of the pattern under AddressSanitizer shows the heap-use-after-free before and a clean run after; the full client was not built or run.

Not covered: the connections that pile up in `createProtocolConnections()` on every connect, and the kernel deadlock from #2933.

comments.issue_title: Custom SSH port is ignored on macOS and Windows
comments.body:
I can reproduce this on macOS with AmneziaVPN 5.1.0.6 (build ac175c8, Nov 2, 2026).

The self-hosted server was configured with a custom SSH port (2222). A packet capture on the server showed repeated TCP SYNs from the desktop client to port 22, not 2222. At the time, sshd was listening on 2222 only, so the connection timed out before SSH authentication.

The same RSA key succeeds with the system SSH client on the configured port. This points to the connection target port, rather than key parsing, as the cause of this 305 timeout. After enabling SSH on port 22 while keeping 2222 enabled, SSH key login succeeded on both ports. I have not yet confirmed the Amnezia app’s result after that workaround.

This seems to confirm the reported behavior on a newer macOS build. It may help to log/assert the requested port, the effective libssh session port, and the first TCP destination port, as suggested above.

issues.title: [Bug] Hyphen in Outbound Name Causes Parsing Issue in Hysteria 2
issues.body: There is an issue in Hysteria 2 core where using a hyphen (`-`) in an outbound name causes a parsing problem when referenced in rules. For example, if an outbound is named `New-turkey` and later used in rules like `New-turkey(geosite:cn)`, the core fails to process it correctly and crashes. The issue seems to be caused by the hyphen interfering with the parsing logic. This should either be fixed or documented as a limitation.

issues.title: fix(acl): allow hyphens in outbound names
issues.body:
ACL rules are parsed with `linePattern` in `extras/outbounds/acl/parse.go`, which only accepts `\w+` as the outbound name, so a rule like `New-turkey(geosite:cn)` fails with "invalid syntax" even though the server config happily accepts an outbound with that name. After parsing, the name is only used for a lowercased map lookup, so allowing `-` in the pattern is all it takes.

I kept this to hyphens as the issue describes. Names with other characters such as dots still don't parse, same as before.

The new `TestParseTextRules` case fails on master with `invalid syntax at line 2: New-turkey(geosite:cn)` and passes with this change. `gofumpt -l -extra .` is clean, and `go test ./...` passes in `extras/outbounds` and `app/cmd`.

Fixes #1323

issues.title: Gecko/Salamander PacketConn wrappers disable UDP batching and GSO on Linux
issues.body:
### Summary

The Gecko/Salamander UDP wrappers do not implement the full `OOBCapablePacketConn` interface expected by the bundled quic-go. As a result, `wrapConn` selects `basicConn`, losing UDP batch receive and GSO transmit support even when the underlying Linux UDP socket supports them.

This appears to be an optimization integration gap in the obfuscation wrapper. No change to the protocol or the obfuscation wire format seems necessary.

### Environment and method

- Hysteria source tag: `app/v2.14.0`.
- Go: `go1.26.8`, `CGO_ENABLED=0`.
- Linux 6.12.x, ARM64 receiver and amd64 sender.
- Approximately 1 Gbit/s path, approximately 150 ms RTT.
- Gecko with the default 512/1200 handshake size bounds.
- Single QUIC connection. Download tests with 64 MiB stream / 128 MiB connection receive windows to avoid a small flow-control window masking the IO behavior.
- Temporary instrumented builds; CPU profiles cover 20-second intervals. The built-in time-based download test runs for 26 seconds.

### Source-level cause

In `extras/obfs/conn.go`, `obfsPacketConnUDP` forwards `SyscallConn` and socket buffer methods, but does not provide `ReadMsgUDP` / `WriteMsgUDP`. The outer Gecko wrapper in `extras/obfs/gecko.go` also exposes only packet-at-a-time IO.

In the bundled quic-go's `sys_conn.go`, failure of the `OOBCapablePacketConn` assertion selects `basicConn`. Its capabilities do not include GSO. Forwarding `SyscallConn` alone therefore does not preserve the full UDP optimization path.

### Measurements

With the original transport path:

- Built-in download test: approximately 550 Mbit/s.
- Sender CPU profile: approximately 34 CPU-seconds during 20 seconds of wall time.
- The `sendto` call path accounts for approximately 43% of sender CPU samples.
- AES-GCM encryption accounts for approximately 2% of sender CPU samples.

An experimental Linux adapter implements `ReadBatch`, `ReadMsgUDP`, and `WriteMsgUDP`. On GSO sends it obfuscates each segment separately, retains an independent Salamander salt for each resulting datagram, and adjusts `UDP_SEGMENT` for the salt overhead. Long-header packets retain the existing Gecko fragmentation/reassembly behavior.

That experimental build reached approximately 690 Mbit/s in the same built-in workload, with approximately 17 sender CPU-seconds per 20 seconds of wall time. Counters confirmed actual GSO use, averaging roughly 10 datagrams per send.

A separate application-stream control, keeping an unmodified sing-box 1.14.4 client and its configuration fixed, gave approximately 550–560 Mbit/s with the original server path and 710–730 Mbit/s with the experimental server in repeated runs.

**Attribution limit:** the experimental build also replaces the scalar Salamander XOR loop with equivalent word-wise operations. These measurements compare the combined build; they are not an isolated GSO-only benchmark. A receiver-only XOR control produced only a small throughput change, approximately 550 to 570 Mbit/s. Lock-contention profiles did not identify the obfuscator locks as the dominant wait.

### Reproduction outline

1. Run two standard endpoints with Gecko, the receive windows above, and the normal BBR download path.
2. Run `hysteria speedtest --duration 26s --skip-upload` using the normal client configuration.
3. Inspect which raw-connection implementation quic-go selected and capture a sender CPU profile.
4. Compare with a segment-aware batch/GSO adapter, checking both payload throughput and actual batch/GSO counters.

The existing obfuscation tests plus additional Linux tests verified unchanged salted XOR bytes, independent GSO datagram boundaries, and bidirectional interoperability with the original Gecko wrapper, including handshake reassembly.

### Requested direction

Would an opt-in Linux batch/GSO-capable obfuscation adapter be acceptable? It would need explicit segment-aware obfuscation rather than simply exposing the raw socket, and production review for PMTU, ECN/ancillary metadata, fallback
